units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Periodicity: Classification of Elements and the Periodic Law
objectives: Explain why elements are classified and describe the development from Mendeleev's table to the modern periodic table.
State the modern periodic law and relate groups and periods to recurring electronic structure and chemical properties.
units.body:
PERIODICITY — CLASSIFICATION OF ELEMENTS AND THE PERIODIC LAW

As the number of known elements increased, studying each element separately became difficult. Chemists therefore developed systems for classifying elements so that elements with similar properties could be grouped and their behaviour compared. The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number and displays recurring patterns in their physical and chemical properties.

MENDELEEV’S PERIODIC TABLE
Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements largely in order of increasing atomic weight while placing elements with similar chemical properties in the same groups. He left gaps where he believed undiscovered elements belonged and predicted properties of some of them. The later discovery of elements such as gallium and germanium supported the usefulness of his predictions. However, arranging strictly by atomic weight produced anomalies, so some elements were placed out of strict mass order to preserve chemical similarities.

MODERN PERIODIC LAW
Henry Moseley’s work showed that atomic number, rather than atomic weight, is the more fundamental basis for arranging elements. The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. When elements are arranged in increasing atomic number, similar outer-electron arrangements recur at regular intervals and related chemical properties appear in groups.

PERIODS, GROUPS AND ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE
Horizontal rows are periods; vertical columns are groups. Elements in the same group commonly have similar valence-electron arrangements and therefore show related chemical behaviour. Across a period, properties change progressively as nuclear charge and electron arrangement change. Down a group, additional electron shells affect atomic size and other properties. The source compares alkali metals, alkaline-earth metals and halogens: alkali metals have one outer electron and commonly form +1 ions; alkaline-earth metals have two outer electrons and commonly form +2 ions; halogens have seven outer electrons and commonly form -1 ions. Reactivity trends differ between groups, so comparisons must specify the family and trend being discussed.

WHY PERIODIC CLASSIFICATION IS USEFUL
The periodic table helps predict valency, likely ion formation, similarities between elements, and broad physical and chemical behaviour. It provides a systematic reference for studying elements and their compounds. When answering examination questions, distinguish Mendeleev’s periodic law (properties related to atomic weights) from the modern periodic law (properties related to atomic numbers), and explain the role of groups, periods and outer-shell electrons rather than merely memorising definitions.

SOURCE BOUNDARY
This is a lesson draft mapped to the First-Term SS2 Chemistry source’s opening Periodicity section. It does not replace the remaining First-Term topics on periodic trends, redox, ionic theory, electrolysis and electrochemical cells, nor the Second- and Third-Term schemes. The source contains worked examples and diagrams that still require page-level visual review.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Periodic Trends in Physical Properties
objectives: Explain periodic trends in atomic and ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character.
Use nuclear charge, shielding, electron configuration and atomic size to explain comparisons and exceptions.
units.body:
PERIODIC TRENDS IN PHYSICAL PROPERTIES

Many properties of elements depend on electronic configuration and vary periodically with atomic number. Important periodic properties include atomic and ionic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity and metallic character. These trends help explain and predict how atoms form ions and react.

ATOMIC RADIUS
Atomic radius is an estimate of atomic size. Because the electron cloud has no sharp boundary, different measures are used. Covalent radius is approximately half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond. Van der Waals radius is half the distance between neighbouring non-bonded atoms of the same element in adjacent molecules; it is generally larger than covalent radius. Metallic radius is half the internuclear distance between neighbouring atoms in a metallic lattice.

Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right because nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same principal shell. The stronger effective attraction draws the electron cloud closer to the nucleus. Down a group, atomic radius generally increases because additional occupied shells place the outer electrons farther from the nucleus and increase shielding.

IONIC RADIUS AND ISOELECTRONIC SPECIES
A cation forms when an atom loses electrons; its radius is generally smaller than that of the parent atom because the remaining electrons experience greater attraction and a shell may be removed. An anion forms when an atom gains electrons; its radius is generally larger than that of the parent atom because electron-electron repulsion increases while nuclear charge remains unchanged. Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons. Within an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases because the same electron population is attracted more strongly.

IONIZATION ENERGY
Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. Successive ionization energies increase because each electron removed leaves a more positively charged ion that holds its remaining electrons more strongly. A particularly large jump occurs when removal begins to disturb a stable inner-shell configuration after the valence electrons have been removed. Ionization energy is affected by atomic size, nuclear charge, shielding, orbital penetration and electronic configuration. It generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, although subshell stability and electron pairing cause exceptions.

ELECTRON AFFINITY, ELECTRONEGATIVITY AND METALLIC CHARACTER
Electron affinity concerns the energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron. Electronegativity is the relative tendency of an atom in a chemical bond to attract the shared electrons. They are related but not identical. Metallic character describes the tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions; it generally increases down a group and decreases across a period. Halogens tend to gain electrons readily, while noble gases have stable outer-shell configurations and low tendency to react. Trends should be explained using effective nuclear attraction, shielding, atomic size and electron configuration rather than treated as exception-free rules.

EXAM RESPONSE METHOD
When comparing sizes, first determine whether the species are atoms, ions or isoelectronic. For isoelectronic ions, compare nuclear charge. When explaining ionization-energy trends, identify the direction of the trend and state the relevant factors. Distinguish electron affinity (energy change on electron gain) from electronegativity (attraction for shared bonding electrons).

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Concept of Oxidation and Reduction
objectives: Explain oxidation and reduction using classical, electron-transfer and oxidation-number concepts.
Apply oxidation-number rules to identify oxidation, reduction, oxidising agents and reducing agents in reactions.
units.body:
OXIDATION AND REDUCTION — REDOX CONCEPTS AND OXIDATION NUMBERS

Oxidation and reduction occur together in redox reactions. Everyday examples include rusting and combustion; industrial examples include electroplating and metal extraction. The source introduces the classical definitions, electron-transfer definitions and oxidation-number approach.

CLASSICAL AND ELECTRON-TRANSFER DEFINITIONS
In the classical concept, oxidation involves addition of oxygen or an electronegative radical, or removal of hydrogen or an electropositive radical. Reduction involves addition of hydrogen or an electropositive radical, or removal of oxygen or an electronegative radical. In the electron-transfer concept, oxidation is loss of one or more electrons, while reduction is gain of one or more electrons. These occur simultaneously because electrons lost by one reacting species are gained by another. The reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidised; the oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced.

OXIDATION NUMBER
Oxidation number (oxidation state) is a formal value assigned to an atom using agreed rules for allocating bonding electrons. It is useful where electron transfer is not represented as a simple transfer of whole electrons. In a free element, the oxidation number is zero. For a monatomic ion, it equals the ion charge. Fluorine is -1 in its compounds. Hydrogen is usually +1, except in metal hydrides where it is -1. Oxygen is usually -2, but is -1 in peroxides and has positive values in compounds with fluorine. The sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound is zero; in a polyatomic ion, the sum equals the ion charge. Group 1 metals are usually +1 and Group 2 metals usually +2 in compounds.

A rise in oxidation number indicates oxidation; a fall indicates reduction. The oxidising agent undergoes a decrease in oxidation number, while the reducing agent undergoes an increase. A redox reaction can be separated into oxidation and reduction half-reactions: the oxidation half-reaction shows electron loss and the reduction half-reaction shows electron gain. The number of electrons lost and gained must balance when the half-reactions are combined.

HOW TO ANSWER REDOX QUESTIONS
First assign oxidation numbers using the rules, then compare the relevant atoms before and after reaction. An increase identifies oxidation; a decrease identifies reduction. Identify the oxidising agent as the species reduced and the reducing agent as the species oxidised. When a question asks which substance is oxidised or reduced, state the substance and briefly support the answer with the oxidation-number change or oxygen/hydrogen transfer.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Balancing Redox Reactions and Identifying Oxidising and Reducing Agents
objectives: Balance redox equations by the ion-electron or half-reaction method while conserving atoms and charge.
Identify oxidising and reducing agents from electron transfer, oxidation-number changes and the source's stated tests.
units.body:
BALANCING REDOX REACTIONS

A redox equation must conserve both atoms and electrical charge. The ion-electron (half-reaction) method separates the oxidation and reduction processes, balances each half-reaction, equalises the electrons transferred, and then combines the halves.

A reliable sequence is: assign oxidation numbers; identify the atoms whose oxidation numbers change; write oxidation and reduction half-reactions; balance the atoms undergoing change; add electrons to balance charge; balance oxygen with water; balance hydrogen with H+ in acidic solution; for basic solution use water and hydroxide ions to remove excess H+; multiply the half-reactions so that electrons lost equal electrons gained; add and cancel common species. Recheck every atom and the total charge at the end.

An oxidising agent causes another substance to be oxidised and is itself reduced. A reducing agent causes another substance to be reduced and is itself oxidised. The source describes tests involving Fe2+ changing to Fe3+, starch-iodide paper turning blue-black when iodine is produced, acidified permanganate losing its purple colour, and dichromate changing from orange towards green. Interpret these observations through the species that gains or loses electrons; do not identify an agent from colour alone without the reaction context.

The source places identification of oxidising and reducing agents after the Week 4 balancing section, while the scheme lists it as a separate topic. Both are retained in this source-week unit pending detailed scheme/body reconciliation.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Ionic Theory, Electrolytes and Electrical Conductivity
objectives: Explain the ionic theory and the movement of cations and anions in an electric field.
Distinguish ionic, covalent, strong-electrolyte, weak-electrolyte and non-electrolyte behaviour in solid, molten and aqueous states.
units.body:
IONIC THEORY AND ELECTROLYTES

The source attributes ionic theory to Arrhenius (1880). Ionic substances contain positive and negative ions arranged in a crystal lattice. When an ionic substance dissolves in water or melts, its ions become mobile and can carry electric charge. Cations move towards the cathode (negative electrode); anions move towards the anode (positive electrode).

An ionic solid generally does not conduct because its ions are fixed in the lattice. The molten substance or aqueous solution can conduct because ions can move. Metals conduct through mobile electrons, including in the solid state; this is different from ionic conduction. A covalent molecular substance generally consists of neutral molecules and usually does not conduct unless it ionises in solution.

Strong electrolytes ionise or dissociate extensively in aqueous solution; weak electrolytes ionise only partially; non-electrolytes do not produce mobile ions in solution. The source gives strong acids, strong bases and salts as strong-electrolyte examples, ethanoic acid and ammonia solution as weak-electrolyte examples, and glucose and ethanol as non-electrolytes. Water itself ionises only slightly.

The source's coloured-ion demonstration uses copper(II) chromate solution: blue Cu2+ ions migrate towards the cathode, while yellow CrO4 2- ions migrate towards the anode. The observed colour movement demonstrates directional ion migration. Distinguish an electrolyte (a substance conducting through mobile ions with chemical change at electrodes) from a metallic conductor (which carries current through electrons without the same electrolytic decomposition).

An electrovalent (ionic) compound consists of oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Electrolysis and Preferential Discharge of Ions
objectives: Define electrolysis and distinguish electrodes, anode, cathode, cations and anions.
Explain how ion concentration, position in the electrochemical series and electrode material influence preferential discharge.
units.body:
ELECTROLYSIS

Electrolysis is the chemical decomposition of an electrolyte in the molten state or in aqueous solution by passing direct electric current through it. The electrolyte contains mobile ions. The cathode is the negative electrode in an electrolytic cell and attracts cations; reduction occurs there. The anode is the positive electrode and attracts anions; oxidation occurs there.

Cations are positively charged ions and anions are negatively charged ions. An electrode is the conducting surface through which current enters or leaves the electrolyte. A conductor may carry current without being decomposed, whereas an electrolyte undergoes chemical change during electrolysis.

The source discusses preferential (selective) discharge: when several ions can be discharged at an electrode, the product depends on the relative ease of discharge. Relevant factors include the position of the ion in the electrochemical series, the concentration of ions in solution, and whether the electrode is inert or reactive. The source illustrates the contribution of water ionisation and dissolved electrolyte ions when predicting products in aqueous electrolysis.

For every electrolysis question, first list the ions present (including ions from water where relevant), identify the anode and cathode, consider the discharge factors, then write balanced half-equations and check atoms and charge. Do not assume that the products of a molten electrolyte and its aqueous solution are identical.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Electrolytic Cells and Electrolysis of Specified Electrolytes
objectives: Describe the components and operation of an electrolytic cell and predict electrode products for specified electrolytes.
Explain industrial applications of electrolysis, including extraction/refining, electroplating, anodising and water electrolysis.
units.body:
ELECTROLYTIC CELLS AND APPLICATIONS

An electrolytic cell contains an electrolyte in molten or aqueous form, a pair of electrodes, a non-conducting vessel and a direct-current power source. The cathode is connected to the negative terminal and is the site of reduction; the anode is connected to the positive terminal and is the site of oxidation. Product prediction requires identifying the ions present and applying preferential-discharge rules.

The source treats electrolysis of specified electrolytes and describes industrial uses. Electrometallurgy uses electrical energy to extract metals from suitable compounds. Electrorefining purifies a metal: the impure metal is the anode, a thin sheet of pure metal is the cathode, and a solution containing the metal ions is the electrolyte. Metal dissolves from the anode and is deposited at the cathode.

Electroplating coats an object with a thin layer of another metal. The object is the cathode, the coating metal is the anode, and a soluble compound of the coating metal supplies the electrolyte ions. The source also describes anodising aluminium: aluminium is made the anode so that a thicker protective aluminium oxide layer forms.

For acidified water, hydrogen is collected at the cathode and oxygen at the anode; the volume ratio is approximately 2:1. The source describes the use of a Hofmann voltameter to collect the gases separately. A labelled diagram should show the power source, electrodes, electrolyte, polarity and the products at each electrode. Practical setup and safety details require teacher review before classroom use.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Electrochemical Cells and Standard Electrode Potential
objectives: Explain how a galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through separated oxidation and reduction half-reactions.
Calculate cell EMF from standard reduction potentials and explain the role of the standard hydrogen electrode.
units.body:
ELECTROCHEMISTRY AND ELECTRODE POTENTIAL

Electrochemistry studies the relationship and interconversion between chemical and electrical energy. A galvanic (voltaic or electrochemical) cell produces electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction by carrying out oxidation and reduction in separate half-cells. In the Daniell cell, zinc is oxidised and copper(II) ions are reduced; electrons travel through the external circuit from the zinc electrode towards the copper electrode.

A redox couple consists of an oxidised and reduced form of a species. The electrode potential describes the tendency of the corresponding half-cell reaction to occur. Under the convention used in the source, half-reactions are written as reductions. Standard electrode potential is measured under standard conditions: dissolved ions at 1 mol L-1, temperature 298 K, and gases at 1 bar where applicable.

The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is the reference electrode assigned a potential of zero volts. Other standard electrode potentials are measured relative to it. The electrochemical series arranges redox couples by standard reduction potential and helps predict electron flow and the feasibility/direction of redox reactions.

For a cell, E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), using standard reduction potentials for both half-cells. Reduction occurs at the cathode (the higher reduction potential in a spontaneous galvanic cell); oxidation occurs at the anode. Keep the sign convention consistent and do not change the sign of a tabulated reduction potential unless explicitly converting it to an oxidation potential.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Applications of Electrochemical Cells
objectives: Compare primary and secondary cells and explain the source's examples of dry, mercury and lead-storage cells.
Describe fuel-cell and battery applications and relate cell design to the production and storage of electrical energy.
units.body:
APPLICATIONS OF ELECTROCHEMICAL CELLS

Electrochemical cells provide portable electrical energy. A battery is commonly an arrangement of two or more galvanic cells connected together. A useful cell should be compact, maintain a reasonably steady voltage, provide energy for a useful period and, where required, be rechargeable.

Primary cells are not designed to be recharged after their chemical reaction has been used. The source describes the dry (Leclanche) cell, with a zinc container as anode and a graphite rod surrounded by manganese dioxide and carbon as the cathode material. It also describes the mercury cell and its zinc-mercury amalgam anode and mercury(II) oxide/carbon cathode mixture.

Secondary cells can be recharged by passing direct current through them so that the cell reactions are driven in the reverse direction. The lead-storage battery uses spongy lead and lead dioxide electrodes in sulfuric acid electrolyte. During discharge, lead sulfate forms and the acid concentration decreases; recharging reverses the electrode processes. The source also mentions nickel-cadmium storage cells.

Fuel cells convert the chemical energy of a supplied fuel and oxidant into electrical energy. In examination answers, distinguish a cell's electrode materials, electrolyte, discharge reaction, rechargeability and typical use. The source's diagrams and full electrode equations require page-level visual and technical checking before delivery.

units.title: Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis and Quantitative Calculations
objectives: Calculate electric charge passed during electrolysis using Q = I x t and relate charge to moles of electrons.
Apply Faraday's first and second laws to calculate deposited or liberated mass using chemical equivalents.
units.body:
FARADAY'S LAWS OF ELECTROLYSIS

Electric charge passed during electrolysis is Q = I x t, where Q is measured in coulombs, I in amperes and t in seconds. One ampere is one coulomb per second. Always convert minutes and hours to seconds before substituting values.

Faraday's first law states that the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte, provided the relevant conditions are fixed. Faraday's second law compares the masses of different substances liberated by the same quantity of electricity: the masses are proportional to their chemical equivalents.

One Faraday is the charge carried by one mole of electrons, approximately 96,500 C. The chemical equivalent is the molar mass divided by the number of electrons transferred per ion or formula unit. A useful calculation relationship is m = (M x I x t)/(n x F), where M is molar mass, n is the number of electrons per ion, and F is the Faraday constant.

For each problem: write the electrode half-equation; determine n; convert time to seconds; calculate Q; use the electron stoichiometry or Faraday's law; include units; and check that the result is physically reasonable. The source's worked examples include copper deposition and oxygen liberation from aqueous copper(II) sulfate, and aluminium deposition from fused aluminium oxide. The printed numerical examples and equations should receive a separate arithmetic review.

units.title: Rate of Chemical Reaction
objectives: Define rate of reaction and interpret a rate curve.
Explain collision theory and factors affecting reaction rate.
units.body:
RATE OF REACTION

The rate of a chemical reaction measures how quickly reactants are used or products are formed. It can be expressed as the change in concentration, amount or mass over the time taken. The source gives rate as change in concentration divided by time, with units such as mol dm-3 s-1; where mass is measured, units such as g s-1 may be used. Always state which measured quantity is being used.

Reaction rate can be followed by measuring mass loss, volume of gas produced, precipitate formation, colour intensity, pH or pressure as time passes. A rate curve is steepest when the reaction is fastest and becomes less steep as reactants are used. A horizontal section indicates that no further measurable change is occurring. The gradient at a point represents instantaneous rate; an average rate is total change divided by total time.

Collision theory states that reacting particles must collide with sufficient energy to overcome activation energy. Not every collision is effective. Rate is affected by the nature and concentration of reactants, gas pressure, surface area, temperature, light in photochemical reactions and catalysts. For a fair comparison, change one factor while keeping the others constant.

units.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions; Thermodynamics
objectives: Distinguish exothermic and endothermic reactions using heat transfer and enthalpy change.

units.body:
THERMOCHEMISTRY AND THERMODYNAMICS

An exothermic reaction transfers heat from the reacting system to the surroundings and has a negative enthalpy change. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings and has a positive enthalpy change. The source discusses heat content (enthalpy), heats of reaction, standard heat of formation and neutralisation, and the energy changes associated with chemical processes.

The first law of thermodynamics expresses conservation of energy: energy is not created or destroyed, but transferred or converted. Using the chemistry sign convention, the change in internal energy is related to heat and work by Delta U = q + w, where q is positive when heat enters the system and w is positive when work is done on the system. If the system does work on the surroundings, w is negative.

The second law connects spontaneity with the entropy change of the system and surroundings. Entropy is a measure of energy dispersal or disorder. A spontaneous process has an overall increase in entropy of the universe. Enthalpy, entropy and temperature must be considered together; do not decide spontaneity from heat release alone.

units.title: Chemical Equilibrium and Le Chatelier's Principle
objectives: Explain reversible reactions and dynamic chemical equilibrium.
Apply Le Chatelier's principle to changes in temperature and pressure for gaseous equilibria.
units.body:
CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM

A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and reverse directions. In a closed system, dynamic equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. The concentrations of reactants and products then remain constant, although both reactions continue at the particle level.

Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the equilibrium position shifts in the direction that tends to oppose the disturbance. Adding a reactant or removing a product generally favours the forward direction; adding product or removing reactant favours the reverse direction.

For gaseous equilibria, increasing pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas, while decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas molecules. Temperature effects depend on whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic: increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the equilibrium position or equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature.

OXYGEN AND OXIDES

Oxygen is a reactive non-metal and a member of Group 16. The source covers the electronic structure and bonding of oxygen, its general properties, laboratory and industrial preparation, and its uses. Oxygen supports combustion and reacts with many elements to form oxides. In chemical equations, identify the reactants and products and balance the atoms on both sides.

Oxides are binary compounds containing oxygen combined with another element. The source introduces classification by chemical behaviour: basic oxides (commonly metal oxides) react with acids to form salt and water; acidic oxides (commonly non-metal oxides) react with bases; amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases; neutral oxides show neither typical acidic nor basic behaviour. Use the reaction, not only the element type, to justify classification.

The source's week evaluation asks for properties of oxygen and its chemical reactions. Its general revision also links oxides with air pollution and electrolysis questions from earlier learning. Keep oxygen preparation, reactions and oxide classification distinct when organising answers.

objectives: Describe the electronic configuration and trends of the halogens.

units.body:
CHLORINE AND THE HALOGENS

The halogens are Group 17 elements with seven electrons in their outer shell. They tend to gain one electron to form halide ions with a -1 charge. Their physical properties and reactivity show trends down the group. The source compares the electronic configuration and physical and chemical properties of halogens, and covers laboratory and industrial preparation of chlorine.

Chlorine is a reactive gas and a strong oxidising agent. It reacts with metals and non-metals and is used for disinfection and in chemical manufacture. Hydrogen chloride gas dissolves readily in water to form hydrochloric acid. The source describes hydrogen chloride as a colourless gas with an irritating smell that fumes in moist air and turns moist blue litmus red.

Chlorides are salts formed when the hydrogen ion of hydrochloric acid is replaced by a metal or other suitable cation. Many chlorides are soluble, but silver chloride and lead(II) chloride are common exceptions under ordinary conditions. For a chloride test, acidify the sample with dilute nitric acid and add silver nitrate; a white precipitate of silver chloride indicates chloride ions.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Nitrogen
objectives: Describe the physical and chemical properties, preparation and uses of nitrogen.
Explain the main stages of the nitrogen cycle and represent key transformations with equations.
units.body:
NITROGEN

Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless gas that makes up most of the Earth's atmosphere. Its molecules contain a strong triple bond, which makes nitrogen relatively unreactive at ordinary temperatures. The source covers the general properties of Group 15 elements, laboratory and industrial preparation of nitrogen, and its uses.

Nitrogen is used where an inert atmosphere is needed, in food packaging and in industrial processes. It is also an essential element in proteins and other biological molecules. Atmospheric nitrogen cannot be used directly by most plants; it must be converted into soluble nitrogen compounds through biological and non-biological processes.

The nitrogen cycle links atmospheric nitrogen, soil compounds and living organisms. Nitrogen fixation converts nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen compounds; plants assimilate nitrogen compounds; animals obtain nitrogen by feeding; decomposition returns nitrogen compounds to soil; nitrification and denitrification transform nitrogen compounds and return nitrogen to the atmosphere. The source describes lightning-related oxidation of atmospheric nitrogen and the formation of nitrogen oxides and acids.

objectives: Describe the preparation, properties and uses of ammonia.
Explain the preparation and reactions of trioxonitrate(V) acid and important nitrogen oxides.
units.body:
COMPOUNDS OF NITROGEN

The source covers oxides of nitrogen, ammonia and trioxonitrate(V) acid. Ammonia (NH3) is a colourless gas with a pungent smell and is very soluble in water, forming an alkaline solution. It is prepared industrially by the Haber process from nitrogen and hydrogen under controlled conditions, and the source also describes laboratory preparation.

Ammonia reacts with acids to form ammonium salts and can act as a reducing agent in some reactions. Its uses include manufacture of fertilisers and other nitrogen compounds. When writing equations, identify the reactant conditions and balance the atoms.

Trioxonitrate(V) acid (HNO3) is a strong acid and an oxidising agent. The source describes laboratory preparation by displacing it from a nitrate salt (such as potassium nitrate) using concentrated sulfuric acid, with an all-glass apparatus because the acid vapour attacks cork and rubber. Nitrogen oxides have different oxidation states and properties; classify them carefully and use balanced equations to show their reactions.

units.title: Sulphur and Its Allotropes
objectives: Describe the physical properties, extraction and uses of sulphur.
Distinguish rhombic and monoclinic sulphur and explain allotropy.
units.body:
SULPHUR

Sulphur is a yellow non-metallic solid. The source states that it is insoluble in water, soluble in some non-polar solvents such as carbon disulfide, and a poor conductor of heat and electricity. It melts at about 119 degrees Celsius and boils at about 444 degrees Celsius. Sulphur occurs in different allotropic forms.

The source identifies rhombic and monoclinic sulphur and asks learners to compare their properties and transition temperature. Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different structural forms in the same physical state. The forms differ in arrangement and stability over temperature ranges; avoid treating them as different elements.

The Frasch process extracts underground sulphur by using superheated water to melt the sulphur and compressed air to force molten sulphur to the surface. When describing the process, identify the pipes and the roles of hot water and compressed air. The source's evaluation also asks learners to compare the two allotropes and describe extraction.

objectives: Describe the preparation and properties of hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide.
Outline the Contact Process for manufacturing tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid.
units.body:
COMPOUNDS OF SULPHUR

The source covers hydrogen sulphide (H2S), sulphur dioxide (SO2), sulphur trioxide (SO3) and tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (H2SO4). Hydrogen sulphide is a poisonous gas with a characteristic rotten-egg smell; it can be prepared in the laboratory by reacting a metal sulphide with a dilute acid. It behaves as a reducing agent and can be oxidised to sulphur or sulphur dioxide.

Sulphur dioxide is produced by burning sulphur in air and is a colourless, choking gas. It dissolves in water to form an acidic solution and acts as a reducing agent; it is also used in bleaching and preservation. Sulphur trioxide reacts vigorously with water to form sulfuric acid, so industrial production uses controlled absorption.

The Contact Process includes burning sulphur or roasting sulphide ores to form SO2, purifying and drying the gas, catalytic oxidation of SO2 to SO3 (commonly using vanadium(V) oxide), and absorption of SO3 in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum, which is diluted to the required acid concentration.

units.title: Water: Structure, Hardness and Treatment
objectives: Describe sources, types, structure and laboratory tests for water.
Explain temporary and permanent hardness and outline municipal water treatment.
units.body:
WATER

The source covers natural water sources (rain, wells, springs and sea water) and treated water (distilled, pipe-borne and chlorinated water). It distinguishes soft water, which forms lather readily with soap, from hard water, which does not. Hardness is associated with dissolved calcium and magnesium salts.

Temporary hardness is associated with hydrogentrioxocarbonate salts such as calcium hydrogentrioxocarbonate and can be removed by boiling or by adding suitable lime. Permanent hardness is associated with soluble calcium or magnesium sulphates and chlorides and can be reduced by chemical precipitation or ion-exchange methods. Hard water wastes soap and can cause scale in boilers, but calcium salts can contribute to dietary mineral intake.

The source describes municipal treatment by coagulation, sedimentation, filtration and chlorination. Coagulation forms flocs; sedimentation allows them to settle; filtration removes remaining suspended matter; chlorination disinfects the water. It also describes tests using anhydrous copper(II) sulphate and cobalt(II) chloride paper; these indicate water presence but are not specific to pure water.

units.title: Solubility and Solutions
objectives: Define solubility and distinguish saturated and unsaturated solutions.
Calculate solubility in mass and molar concentration units and interpret temperature effects.
units.body:
SOLUBILITY AND SOLUTIONS

Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a specified amount of solvent at a stated temperature to form a saturated solution. An unsaturated solution contains less than the maximum amount and can dissolve more solute under the same conditions. A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute at the stated temperature.

Solubility is commonly expressed as grams of solute per cubic decimetre of solvent or solution, or as moles per cubic decimetre. Convert volumes carefully: 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3. To convert a mass concentration to molar concentration, divide the mass concentration by the molar mass of the solute.

Solubility curves show how the amount dissolved varies with temperature. Cooling a saturated solution may cause excess solute to crystallise if solubility decreases. Gas solubility generally decreases as temperature increases and increases with pressure. The source includes calculations involving potassium chloride and lead(II) trioxonitrate(V); retain units and distinguish solvent volume from solution volume.

units.title: Mass/Volume Relationships and Stoichiometry
objectives: Explain mole, relative atomic mass, relative molecular mass and stoichiometry.

units.body:
MASS AND VOLUME RELATIONSHIPS

Stoichiometry is the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation. The mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of specified particles. Relative atomic mass compares the average mass of an atom with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; relative molecular mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule.

To solve a reacting-mass problem, write and balance the equation, convert the known mass to moles using n = m/M, use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, and convert the required moles to mass or volume. For gases at the same temperature and pressure, volume ratios follow the coefficients in the balanced equation. At STP, use the molar gas volume specified in the source or question.

The source includes combustion of ethane, gas-volume calculations and conversions between mass, moles and volume. Identify any limiting reactant and any excess reactant remaining; do not assume all supplied reactants are consumed.

units.body:
ACID AND BASE REACTIONS

The source covers preparation of standard solutions, acid-base indicators and calculations based on acid-base titration. A standard solution has a known concentration. To prepare one accurately, calculate the required amount of solute or dilution volume, measure it with suitable apparatus, dissolve or dilute safely, transfer quantitatively to a volumetric flask, make up to the calibration mark and mix thoroughly.

An acid-base indicator changes colour over a pH range. The source compares methyl orange and phenolphthalein for different acid/base combinations. Choose an indicator whose colour-change range lies within the steep pH change near the equivalence point. Record initial and final burette readings and use concordant titres for calculations.

For titration calculations, write the balanced reaction and use the mole relationship from its coefficients. For a 1:1 acid-base reaction, moles acid = moles base at equivalence; for other ratios, include the stoichiometric coefficients. The source's request for a 0.05 mol dm-3 sulfuric acid solution does not specify stock concentration or final volume, so an exact dilution volume cannot be calculated without those data.

units.body:
INTRODUCTION TO ORGANIC CHEMISTRY

Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, especially those containing carbon-hydrogen bonds. Carbon is tetravalent and forms strong covalent bonds with itself and other elements. This catenation allows carbon atoms to form straight chains, branched chains and rings, with single, double or triple bonds.

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by a CH2 unit. Members have similar chemical properties and show gradual changes in physical properties. A functional group is an atom or group of atoms responsible for characteristic reactions; examples include hydroxyl (-OH), carboxyl (-COOH) and carbon-carbon double bonds (C=C).

Saturated compounds contain carbon-carbon single bonds only, while unsaturated compounds contain at least one carbon-carbon double or triple bond. The source covers classification of hydrocarbons and structural formulae. When writing formulae, show the correct valency of carbon and distinguish molecular, condensed and displayed structural formulae.

units.title: Alkanes
objectives: Use IUPAC rules to name and write structures of simple alkanes and their isomers.
Describe the preparation, physical properties and chemical reactions of methane and other alkanes.
units.body:
ALKANES

Alkanes are saturated aliphatic hydrocarbons containing carbon-carbon single bonds. Their general formula for an open-chain molecule is CnH2n+2. The source covers IUPAC nomenclature, laboratory preparation, properties and uses. Select the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent, number it to give substituents the lowest possible locants, name and alphabetise substituents, and use the appropriate alkane suffix.

Methane is the simplest alkane. The source describes its laboratory preparation and chemical properties. Alkanes are relatively unreactive compared with unsaturated hydrocarbons, but they undergo combustion and substitution reactions. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water; limited oxygen may produce carbon monoxide or carbon.

Isomerism occurs when compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements. Structural isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers differ in spatial arrangement. Draw structures carefully, check valency, and use IUPAC names that identify branches and their positions.

practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as an answer printed in the source.
practice.answer: One laboratory method is heating a dry mixture of sodium ethanoate and soda lime (sodium hydroxide mixed with calcium oxide). Decarboxylation produces methane, which can be collected over water because it is only slightly soluble in water.
practice.explanation: The source expects a preparation method; include the reactants, heating and collection of methane.

Explains heating/decarboxylation to form methane.

units.title: Alkenes
objectives: Explain the structure and nomenclature of alkenes and identify the carbon-carbon double bond.
Describe preparation, physical properties, uses and addition reactions of ethene.
units.body:
ALKENES

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond. For open-chain alkenes with one double bond, the general formula is CnH2n. The source focuses on ethene, its nomenclature, preparation, properties and uses. In naming an alkene, choose the longest chain containing the double bond and number it so the double bond receives the lowest possible locant.

The carbon-carbon double bond makes alkenes more reactive than alkanes in characteristic addition reactions. Ethene undergoes hydrogenation, halogen addition, addition of hydrogen halides and hydration under suitable conditions. Bromine water is decolourised by an alkene; acidified potassium permanganate can also be decolourised under suitable test conditions.

Ethene is a colourless gas and is used in the manufacture of polymers and other chemicals, and in fruit ripening. The source asks for laboratory preparation and physical properties. When describing a laboratory setup, identify the reactants, temperature conditions, gas purification/drying and safe collection method.

practice.question_locator: Third-Term Chemistry source, Week 7 EVALUATION, item 1.
practice.question: How would you prepare a jar of ethene gas in the laboratory?
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as an answer printed in the source.
practice.answer: Heat ethanol with concentrated sulfuric acid at about 170 degrees Celsius to dehydrate it, producing ethene and water. Pass the gas through a suitable wash/drying arrangement to remove impurities and collect it over water, since ethene is only slightly soluble in water.
practice.explanation: The response should identify dehydration of ethanol and suitable gas collection; apparatus details require visual comparison with the source diagram.

marking.criterion: Identifies ethanol and concentrated sulfuric acid.
States heating/dehydration to form ethene.
Describes purification and suitable collection.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Alkynes and Aromatic Hydrocarbons
objectives: Describe the structure, nomenclature and preparation of alkynes such as ethyne.
Explain the structure of benzene, resonance and selected preparation methods.
units.body:
ALKYNES AND BENZENE

Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon triple bond. The general formula for an open-chain alkyne with one triple bond is CnH2n-2. Ethyne (acetylene) is the simplest alkyne. The source covers nomenclature, preparation, properties and uses, then introduces aromatic hydrocarbons and the structure of benzene.

The triple bond allows alkynes to undergo addition reactions. Ethyne burns in oxygen and can undergo hydrogenation and addition with halogens and hydrogen halides. Laboratory preparation commonly involves reacting calcium carbide with water to produce ethyne and calcium hydroxide; the gas must be handled with appropriate precautions because it is highly flammable.

Benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon with formula C6H6. Its structure is represented by resonance forms with delocalised pi electrons around the ring; the actual molecule is a resonance hybrid rather than alternating fixed single and double bonds. The source asks learners to describe benzene preparation and draw resonance structures.

practice.question_locator: Third-Term Chemistry source, Week 8 EVALUATION, item 1.
practice.question: Describe three methods of preparing benzene.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as an answer printed in the source.
practice.answer: Common preparations include trimerisation of ethyne (3C2H2 -> C6H6), dehydrogenation of cyclohexane to benzene, and decarboxylation of sodium benzoate with soda lime to form benzene.
practice.explanation: The three methods should be supported by appropriate reactants or equations; match the exact methods emphasised in the source lesson before certification.

marking.criterion: Describes trimerisation of ethyne.
Describes dehydrogenation of cyclohexane.
Describes decarboxylation of sodium benzoate.

practice.question: Draw the resonance structures of benzene.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as an answer printed in the source.

practice.explanation: The two Kekule structures are equivalent contributors; the circle representation denotes delocalisation and is not a separate fixed bond arrangement.

units.subject: Chemistry
units.title: Alkanols and Ethanol
objectives: Describe the structure, classification and nomenclature of alkanols.
Explain ethanol production by fermentation and its physical properties, uses and chemical reactions.
units.body:
ALKANOLS

Alkanols are organic compounds containing a hydroxyl (-OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon atom. They may be classified by the number of hydroxyl groups and by the type of carbon atom bearing the hydroxyl group. The source covers types and classes, industrial production by fermentation, properties and uses.

Ethanol is a colourless, volatile liquid that mixes with water and has a characteristic smell. It can be produced by fermentation of sugars using yeast under controlled conditions with limited oxygen. Enzymes in yeast convert glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Starchy materials must first be converted to fermentable sugars before fermentation.

Ethanol undergoes combustion, oxidation and reactions characteristic of the hydroxyl group. It is used as a solvent, fuel and chemical feedstock. In exam answers, distinguish fermentation from hydration of ethene as two different production routes, and write balanced equations for the reactions requested.

practice.question_locator: Third-Term Chemistry source, Week 9 EVALUATION, item 1.
practice.question: Describe fully the production of ethanol from a named starchy material or food.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not represented as an answer printed in the source.
practice.answer: For cassava, first grate and process the starch-rich material, then gelatinise and hydrolyse the starch to fermentable sugars using suitable enzymes. Cool the sugar solution, add yeast and allow anaerobic fermentation to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. Distil the fermented mixture to separate and concentrate the ethanol.
practice.explanation: A complete answer identifies the starchy feedstock, conversion of starch to sugar, yeast fermentation and distillation; industrial details require subject review.

marking.criterion: Names a starchy feedstock and describes conversion to fermentable sugar.
Explains yeast fermentation under limited oxygen.
States distillation to recover ethanol.
